references.text: Context for the Samaritans' faith: Many of the Samaritans in the town had come to believe because of the woman's testimony ([ref:Joh 4:39|John 4:39]), and this led them to go out to Jesus and ask him to stay with them.

Result of Jesus' stay: The two days Jesus spent with the Samaritans led even more people to believe, no longer just because of what the woman said, but because they had heard him themselves ([ref:Joh 4:41-42|John 4:41–42]).

Parallel to the disciples' first meeting with Jesus, where they were also invited to stay with him and remained that day ([ref:Joh 1:38-39|John 1:38–39]). In both cases, being together with Jesus leads to deeper faith.
Jesus stays two days after receiving news of Lazarus' illness ([ref:Joh 11:6|John 11:6]). Both texts specifically mention "two days" as a period of significance in Jesus' ministry.
The Samaritans' reception of the gospel in Acts confirms the pattern from Samaria: Philip preached Christ to the Samaritans, and they received the message with joy ([ref:Apg 8:5-8|Acts 8:5–8]).
Lydia asked Paul and his companions to stay at her house after she came to believe ([ref:Apg 16:15|Acts 16:15]). The same pattern as in Samaria: faith leads to an invitation to stay.

The disciples on the road to Emmaus urged Jesus to stay with them ([ref:Luk 24:29|Luke 24:29]). Just as the Samaritans asked Jesus to stay, people recognize something in Jesus' presence that makes them want him to remain with them.

Jesus stands at the door and knocks – if anyone opens, he will come in and eat with them ([ref:Åp 3:20|Revelation 3:20]). The Samaritans' invitation for Jesus to stay illustrates this mutual hospitality between Jesus and believers.

Jesus stayed with Zacchaeus and remained at his house ([ref:Luk 19:5-6|Luke 19:5–6]). Zacchaeus welcomed Jesus with joy, just as the Samaritans asked Jesus to stay – in both cases, Jesus' presence leads to salvation.
